coach_says: Good move. f5 kicks the bishop off its central post on e4 and grabs space in front of your king, and it is as good as anything else here. White can take on b7, but your pieces stay active and you stay clearly better.

Fine. The knight on h7 is stuck: your bishop and both rooks on the h-file aim at it, so it will fall whatever Black does. Taking it straight away with Bxh7+ is the simplest way to cash in, but Bd3 keeps that capture ready and you are still winning easily.

Well played. Your bishop on d3 was attacked by the e4 pawn, and instead of just moving it you first hit the rook on f6 with Ng4, gaining time. After the rook moves, Bxe4 saves the bishop. That is a useful in-between move.

You are a pawn up in a rook ending, and in rook endings the active rook matters most. After f4 the black rook just steps to e4, attacks your f-pawn, then goes to c4 to hit c2, and your rook ends up on d2 defending. Rd4 first puts your rook to work: it guards d5 and attacks the b4 pawn, so Black has to answer that, and you can play f4 afterwards.

Bxd4 grabs a pawn, but the bishop on d4 is only protected by the knight on e2, and that knight is attacked by the rook on c2. Black plays Rxe2, and after Qxe2 Rxd4 you have given a bishop and a knight for a rook, your d3 and f4 pawns are weak and Black's pieces flood in. Before you capture, check what defends the capturing piece and whether that defender can be taken. Here the first job was to deal with the rook on your second rank with Rc1.
